title: Genesis 27. The Cup Stolen.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 27. The Cup Stolen.
When Isaac was old,
and his eyes were dim so that he could not see,
he called Esau his older son.
My son.
Here I am.
See, I am old.
I do not know the day of my death.
Now take your weapons, your quiver and your bow,
and go out to the field and hunt game for me.
Prepare savory food for me, such as I love,
and bring it to me, that I may eat,
and that my soul may bless you before I die.
The Cup of blessing,
the authority of the father to speak the promise over the next generation,
is about to be poured.
Isaac is blind.
The man whose father saw stars and counted dust cannot see his own sons.
The vessel that carried the covenant has lost its sight.
And the first thing he does with his blindness is try to pour the Cup into the wrong vessel.
He calls Esau.
The older son.
The hunter.
The one God said would serve the younger.
Isaac does not consult God.
He does not consult Rebekah.
He does not remember the oracle that was spoken before the twins were born.
He follows his appetite,
he loves Esau because he eats of his game.
And he wants to eat one more meal and bless the son he loves,
regardless of what God said.
Rebekah was listening.
The woman who drew water at the well,
who said I will go, who entered Sarah's tent,
who was loved by Isaac, overhears.
She remembers.
The oracle: the older shall serve the younger.
The word God spoke before the boys were born.
The word that Rebekah received when she inquired of the Lord.
She knows which son the promise belongs to.
And she takes matters into her own hands.
The same pattern as Sarah giving Hagar.
Human arrangement instead of waiting for God.
The woman who carries the knowledge of what God said now engineers the fulfillment of what God said,
without asking God.
The oracle will prove true.
But the path to it goes through deception.
She speaks to Jacob:
I heard your father speak to Esau your brother, saying,
Bring me game and prepare savory food for me,
that I may eat and bless you before the Lord before I die.
Now therefore, my son, obey my voice.
Go to the flock and bring me two good young goats.
I will prepare them as your father loves.
You bring them to him, that he may eat,
so that he may bless you before he dies.
Jacob hesitates.
Not because it is wrong, because it might fail.
Behold, Esau my brother is a hairy man,
and I am a smooth man.
What if my father touches me?
I will seem to him as a deceiver,
and I would bring a curse on myself and not a blessing.
The grabber calculates.
The man who grabbed a heel and grabbed a birthright now assesses the risk of grabbing a blessing.
His objection is not moral, it is practical.
What if I get caught?
The Cup that was taken by a bowl of stew is now about to be taken by a bowl of stew,
the same recipe, the same trick, the same man.
Rebekah says: Let your curse be on me, my son.
Only obey my voice and go.
The mother takes the risk.
The son takes the blessing.
The woman who was told the older shall serve the younger now arranges for the younger to steal what God said would be his.
The Cup that God promised to Jacob is taken by Jacob before God gives it.
The same impatience as Sarah.
The same arrangement.
The same refusal to wait for the One who spoke the word to fulfill the word.
She takes Esau's best garments, which were with her in the house,
and puts them on Jacob.
She puts the skins of the young goats on his hands and on the smooth of his neck.
She gives the savory food and the bread into his hand.
The disguise is total.
The clothes of the older.
The skin of the goat.
The food the father loves.
The smell of the field.
Every sense that Isaac still has, touch, taste, smell,
is weaponized against him.
The father who cannot see is now surrounded by lies that speak to every sense he has left.
Jacob comes to his father: My father.
Here I am.
Who are you, my son?
Jacob said to his father: I am Esau your firstborn.
I have done as you told me.
Now arise, sit and eat of my game,
that your soul may bless me.
The lie is spoken.
Not by the mother now.
By Jacob.
The man who grabbed a heel and grabbed a birthright now speaks with his own mouth:
I am Esau.
The first lie in Genesis that is spoken directly to a father by a son.
The same verb used for the serpent, the subtle one,
is the root of Jacob's name.
And he uses it.
Isaac said: How is it that you have found it so quickly,
my son?
He said: Because the Lord your God granted me success.
Jacob invokes God.
The man who is lying about his identity names God as the reason his lie succeeded.
The Cup that was sworn by God's name is now stolen under God's name.
The same God who walked through the pieces alone is now cited as the helper of a deception.
Isaac said: Come near, that I may feel you, my son,
whether you are really my son Esau or not.
Jacob went near.
Isaac felt him and said: The voice is Jacob's voice,
but the hands are the hands of Esau.
The blind father hears what the deception cannot hide.
The voice.
The one thing Rebekah could not change.
Isaac hears Jacob, the quiet man, the tent-dweller,
the one who speaks softly,
and the sound does not match the skin.
But the touch wins.
The hands are hairy.
The smell is Esau's.
And Isaac, who was suspicious,
chooses the evidence of his fingers over the evidence of his ears.
He did not recognize him.
He blessed him.
Are you really my son Esau?
I am.
Bring it near to me,
and I will eat of my son's game,
that my soul may bless you.
He brought it near.
Isaac ate.
He drank wine.
And then: Come near now, and kiss me, my son.
Jacob came near and kissed him.
Isaac smelled the smell of his garments and blessed him: See,
the smell of my son is as the smell of a field that the Lord has blessed.
May God give you of the dew of heaven,
of the fatness of the earth, and plenty of grain and wine.
Let peoples serve you, and nations bow down to you.
Be lord over your brothers.
Let your mother's sons bow down to you.
Cursed be everyone who curses you,
and blessed be everyone who blesses you.
The Cup is poured.
The blessing that was meant for the older is spoken over the younger.
The words that carry the promise, dew, fatness, grain, wine, peoples serving,
nations bowing, are given to Jacob.
The same language God used with Abraham: nations, blessing.
The blessing has been stolen.
The father who was blind poured the Cup into the hands of a deceiver wearing goatskins.
As soon as Isaac had finished blessing Jacob,
and Jacob had just gone out from the presence of Isaac his father,
Esau his brother came in from his hunting.
The timing is exact.
Jacob leaves.
Esau enters.
The two sons who struggled in the womb pass each other at the door of a blind father's tent.
The same struggle, but now with words, with weeping,
with a sound that will echo through the rest of Genesis.
Esau also prepared savory food and brought it to his father:
Let my father arise and eat of his son's game,
that your soul may bless me.
Isaac his father said: Who are you?
I am your son, your firstborn, Esau.
Isaac trembled violently.
Who, then, is he who hunted game and brought it to me?
I ate it all before you came, and I blessed him.
Yes, and he shall be blessed.
The trembling.
The father who was blind now sees what he has done.
The hands that felt goatskin, the mouth that ate goat stew,
the nose that smelled Esau's garments, all were deceived.
And the blessing cannot be taken back.
The Cup that was poured cannot be unpoured.
Isaac knows it.
He shall be blessed.
What was spoken in deception is now sealed by the authority of the father.
When Esau heard the words of his father,
he cried with an exceedingly great and bitter cry and said:
Bless me, even me also, my father!
The sound.
The firstborn weeping for what was taken.
The man who despised his birthright now wants its blessing.
The hunter who traded the promise for stew now cries for the promise he sold.
The same birthright he treated as worthless is now the thing he weeps to receive.
He said: Is he not rightly named Jacob?
For he has supplanted me these two times.
He took away my birthright, and see,
now he has taken away my blessing.
Have you not reserved a blessing for me?
Isaac answered: I have made him your lord,
and all his brothers I have given to him for servants.
I have sustained him with grain and wine.
What then can I do for you, my son?
Esau said: Have you but one blessing, my father?
Bless me, even me also, my father.
And Esau lifted up his voice and wept.
The weeping of the firstborn.
The sound that fills the tent where Rebekah once drew water and Isaac once was comforted.
The Cup that was stolen has produced grief.
The promise that was taken by deception has produced a brother who weeps and a brother who runs.
Isaac answered Esau: Behold,
your dwelling shall be away from the fatness of the earth and away from the dew of heaven on high.
By your sword you shall live, and you shall serve your brother.
But when you break loose,
you shall toss his yoke from your neck.
The opposite of Jacob's blessing.
Away from the dew.
Away from the fatness.
By the sword.
Serving the brother.
The firstborn who was meant to receive the Cup receives its shadow.
The blessing that was stolen produces a lesser blessing,
a prophecy of servitude and violence and eventual rebellion.
The same oracle, the older shall serve the younger,
is spoken from both sides now.
From Jacob's side: nations shall serve you.
From Esau's side: you shall serve your brother.
The word of God is fulfilled.
But the path to it goes through goatskin and lies.
Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing with which his father blessed him.
Esau said in his heart:
Let the days of mourning for my father approach.
Then I will kill my brother Jacob.
The Cup that was stolen has produced murder.
The same pattern as Cain and Abel,
the older brother who is passed over becomes the older brother who kills.
The birthright that was traded for stew now produces a death sentence.
The promise that God said would go to the younger has arrived,
through deception, through weeping, through a brother planning to kill a brother.
The words of Esau were told to Rebekah.
She sent and called Jacob and said:
Your brother Esau comforts himself by planning to kill you.
Now therefore, my son, obey my voice.
Arise, flee to Laban my brother in Haran.
Stay with him a few days, until your brother's fury turns away,
until your brother's anger turns from you,
and he forgets what you have done to him.
Then I will send and bring you from there.
Why should I be bereaved of you both in one day?
A few days.
Rebekah sends Jacob away expecting a short exile.
A few days until Esau's fury cools.
She will send for him.
She will bring him back.
The mother who arranged the deception now arranges the escape.
The woman who said let your curse be on me now bears the cost,
she will never see Jacob again.
The few days will become twenty years.
Rebekah will die before Jacob returns.
The Cup that was stolen is now carried into exile,
away from the tent, away from the father, away from the brother,
away from the mother who engineered it.
Rebekah said to Isaac:
I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth.
If Jacob takes a wife of the daughters of Heth,
such as these, of the daughters of the land,
what good will my life do me?
She uses Esau's Hittite wives as the excuse to send Jacob away.
The woman who arranged the deception now arranges the reason.
The same pattern as Abraham, finding a wife from the kindred,
not from the Canaanites.
But the reason is not the future.
The reason is survival.
Jacob must run because of what was done in the tent.
The Cup is stolen.
The oracle will prove true, the older does serve the younger.
But the path to the oracle's fulfillment goes through goatskin and lies and a blind father's trembling and a firstborn's weeping and a death threat and an exile that will last twenty years.
The promise that was given by calling, confirmed by stars,
sealed in flesh, tested on a mountain, sworn by oath,
buried in a grave, opened in a tent, inherited through wells,
is now carried out of the household by a man in disguise,
fleeing his brother,
sent by a mother who will never see him again.
The Cup holds.
The vessel runs.
